title: Faithful Christians Have the Happiest Marriages in America
gist: IFS blog summary of its FOCUS-sponsored 'Devout Difference' report: religion's hold on US family life has collapsed (Catholic weddings -74% since 1970), but remaining churchgoers marry more, divorce less, report happier marriages and more sex. Orthodox Catholics (FOCUS alumni) do best; porn and weak parish support are flagged problems.

insights.claim: The authors argue the US is in an epidemic of social isolation driven partly by the digital revolution of the past 15 years, with in-person conversation, teen socializing, community life and sex all declining sharply.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Frames secular demand for community/connection products and a structural headwind for household formation.
insights.quote: Daily in-person conversation, teen socializing, face-to-face community life, and even sex have all declined sharply in recent years.
insights.locator: America is in the midst of

insights.claim: Marriage has become increasingly protective against early death, suicidal thoughts and unhappiness over the past 20 years, per the authors.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Widening marriage premium implies growing divergence in wellbeing/consumption between married and unmarried cohorts.
insights.quote: Marriage has grown increasingly protective against early death, suicidal thoughts, and unhappiness over the past 20 years

insights.claim: Catholic weddings in the US have fallen 74% since 1970, yet churchgoing Catholics and Protestants still marry more, have more children and divorce less than secular peers.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Shrinking but more fertile/stable religious subpopulation shapes long-run demographic composition.
insights.quote: with Catholic weddings falling by 74% since 1970 to the present

insights.claim: US churchgoers are 39% more likely to be married today than non-churchgoers.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Religiosity is a strong marker for household formation demand (housing, family goods).
insights.quote: churchgoers are 39% more likely to be married today

insights.claim: 79% of churchgoing Catholics and 74% of churchgoing Protestants report being very happily married versus 66% of non-religious spouses.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Quantifies a religiosity premium in marital quality that counters secular-liberation narratives.
insights.quote: 79% of churchgoing Catholics and 74% of churchgoing Protestants are very happily married, compared to 66% of non-religious husbands and wives

insights.claim: Spouses who embrace an ethic of marital permanence have 1.85 times higher odds of being happily married.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Commitment norms, not just affiliation, drive outcomes.

insights.claim: Churchgoing spouses have largely escaped the 'sex recession': 62% have sex at least weekly versus 48% of nonreligious spouses, and churchgoers have 1.42 times higher odds of sexual satisfaction.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Contrarian data against the stereotype of religious prudishness; widening religious-secular divide.
insights.quote: a strong majority of churchgoing spouses (62%) having sex at least once a week now, even as sex drops for nonreligious spouses

insights.claim: 25% of churchgoing husbands view pornography monthly or more, versus 35% of husbands who rarely or never attend church; a large minority of Catholic spouses worry their marriage may not last and large Catholic families report added strain.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Identifies unmet needs (porn recovery, parish family support) within religious communities.
insights.quote: a large minority (25%) of churchgoing husbands view pornography monthly or more

insights.claim: Alumni of FOCUS, the largest Catholic collegiate ministry and the report's sponsor, are more likely to marry, be happily married and less likely to worry about their marriage than other Catholics and non-religious young adults.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Orthodox niches outperforming; note sponsor conflict of interest.
insights.quote: The most orthodox sectors of the Catholic Church appear to be the most successful at fostering strong, stable marriages.
